messages.subject: The trouble with data.table
parts:
This post is not about Rhipe at all.  This is not about Rhipe at all!

But, I do often recommend an R package called data.table for many idioms that come up fairly often in MapReduce because data.table does some things faster and easier than any other tool in R.  For example,. rbindlist is blindingly fast compared to rbind.fill from plyr, and key look ups and reductions in data.table are about as fast and easy as it gets.  

That said, the trouble with data.table is it is soooo easy to introduce hard to find bugs in your code.  This was a note that my colleagues had made too.  Earlier this summer I came to the realization that as long as you only used data.table idioms when using data.tables you are fine, but if you mix and match data.table and data.frame concepts you will eventually have problems.  Which is confusing because when you class a data.table object it says c("data.frame", "data.table").  I finally took the time to cook up the demonstration of why data.table with data.frame like interactions is a dangerous tool, and I note it here for my friends in Rhipe.

I think people should forget data.table objects say "data.frame" on them, and here is why:

> data(iris)
> set.seed(1)
> iris$key = unlist(lapply(1:nrow(iris), function(i) paste(sample(letters, 10,replace=TRUE),collapse=""))) 
> d = as.data.table(iris)
> class(d)
[1] "data.table" "data.frame"
> setkeyv(d, "key")
> x = d$Sepal.Length
> y = d$Sepal.Length
> head(x)
[1] 6.2 5.5 6.7 7.9 5.2 6.4
> head(y)
[1] 6.2 5.5 6.7 7.9 5.2 6.4
> y[1] = 2
> setkeyv(d,"Sepal.Width")
> head(x)
[1] 5.0 6.2 6.0 6.0 6.3 5.5
> head(y)
[1] 2.0 5.5 6.7 7.9 5.2 6.4


data.table plays fast and lose with references and promise mechanics in R when it supports operations that make sense with a data.frame. setkeyv sorts d by key files internally.  After that we assign x and y a promise to a reference (I think).  The x and y start the same as they should.  y[1] induces R to resolve the promise and copy Sepal.Length with copy on change mechanics, whereas x is left as a promise to a reference.    A new sorting is induced on the data.table d, and x which has been observed in one order suddenly changes order without being reassigned to the data.table again, but y has remained in the old sorting order! 

This and things like it is the cause of data.table's reputation among some people I know, and I continue to use it because it is fast, but you got to mentally turn off all your data.table like code habits and just look up the data.table only idioms, and when that isn't possible cast out of data.table and go back to data.frame. 

The only thing I dislike about data.table is the author doesn't make any big deal about how some data.frame interactions can look valid, but do completely different things.
